writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, whether an assessment has been made of the likely impact of AI adoption on software development and the wider technology workforce, including projections regarding job displacement, recruitment trends, wage pressures and the effects on associated professions within the sector.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Cabinet Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises that AI is already reshaping the world of work, particularly in software development and the wider technology sector. While there is currently no clear evidence of widespread job displacement attributable to AI across the UK labour market, we recognise that this could change as AI capabilities advance.

Earlier this year, the Government published an initial assessment of the potential impacts of AI on the UK labour market. AI has the potential to deliver substantial productivity gains, but the Government is determined to ensure that these gains translate into better jobs, higher wages and rising living standards for working people.

We will not take these outcomes for granted. The AI Economics Institute will continue to assess the implications of AI for employment and wages, informing the policy decisions necessary to protect the interests of working people and ensure that Britain is prepared for potentially significant changes to the labour market.

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 prohibits unfair commercial practices, including misleading actions and omissions of material information, that are likely to impact the average consumer’s transactional decision.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) is the independent regulator responsible for regulating advertising in the UK, through codes set by the Committees of Advertising Practice (CAP) and Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice (BCAP). writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what criteria her Department used to provide funding to the Bylines Network through the Local News Fund.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Local News Fund offered grants through a competitive bidding process to local news outlets and other eligible organisations, to help ensure the long-term provision of high quality local news.

A Steering Board was appointed through open competition to ensure a degree of independence in government decisions about funding media outlets. All bids to the Local News Fund were assessed on their own individual merits against clear and objective eligibility and bidding criteria, including consideration of the value for money in each bid, with a strategic assessment conducted by the Steering Board and a technical assessment conducted against a published scoring framework. The criteria were agreed in advance with the Steering Board and published in full as part of the bidding process on Find a Grant.

The Fund's eligibility criteria required local news outlet bidders to demonstrate that their content is editorially accountable, that they had a track record of at least 12 months in publishing local news and that they had been registered as a business in the UK for at least 12 months. Third parties seeking to bid for infrastructure funding needed to have been legally incorporated and trading for at least 12 months, with a track record in delivering services or tools in support of the journalism industry or another relevant field (e.g. publishing, advertising).

Alongside this, we are developing common standards and shared infrastructure to make it easier for departments to find, connect and reuse data, including work on common reference data and the API Mandate.

We are also working with departments on practical use cases, including improving access to data to support young people, and developing the National Data Library so that public sector data is easier to discover and use.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what steps she has taken to implement national inclusion standards, national specialist provision packages, digital individual support plans and EHCPs for children of military families with special educational needs.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department recognises that Armed Forces life may present particular challenges for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), and I have engaged directly with military families about the challenges.

Our consultation included proposals for new National Inclusion Standards, setting out support that should be available in every mainstream setting.

We also proposed a nationally consistent set of Specialist Provision Packages to provide comprehensive, evidence-informed support for children and young people with the most complex needs.

An independent Expert Panel has been appointed to oversee the development of the Standards and Packages. The panel has used research evidence and professional expertise to develop them, and gathered the views of parents, carers, children, and young people with lived experience of SEND.

The proposal is that the packages will underpin education, health and care (EHC) plans to help end the postcode lottery in support. Additionally, EHC plans and new Individual Support Plans will be digital, which will support service children by facilitating smoother transitions and improved information sharing when they move between schools or local authorities.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, whether the National Energy System Operator has taken steps to model the potential impact of curtailing gas-fired generation during a period of low wind and high electricity demand on the likelihood of power cuts.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
writtenQuestions.answerText:
During periods of low renewable output, the Government would not expect there to be significant network constraints, unless caused by network outages.

In periods of low renewable output, gas-fired generation would be expected to provide flexible capacity to help meet demand and maintain security of supply, and this capacity is generally sited relatively close to demand (compared to renewable capacity).

As such, the Government would not generally expect curtailment of gas-fired generation in the low-wind, high-demand scenario described.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, what assessment she has made of the adequacy of the availability of electricity imports during periods of low wind affecting Great Britain and neighbouring countries at the same time.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Capacity Market (CM) is the Government’s main mechanism for ensuring security of electricity supply in Great Britain.

All capacity in the CM, including interconnector imports, is de-rated by technology type, so that the amount of capacity secured reflects each technology’s expected availability during times of system stress, including during periods of low wind in Europe, to ensure the Government is securing the capacity needed to maintain electricity security.

The responsibility for determining interconnector de-rating factors sits with the government, who consider inputs from NESO and the DESNZ Panel of Technical Experts before publishing them on gov.uk each Summer.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, what steps she is taking to help support pensioner households in the lowest quintile from spending 12% of their after tax household income on energy bills.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises the pressure energy costs place on low-income households, including pensioners.

We are providing immediate support through the £100 Household Energy Payment, reaching almost 90% of the lowest-income households, and the expanded £150 Warm Home Discount.

This support comes on top of the average £150 of costs reduced from household energy bills and the extension of zero rate of VAT on domestic electricity to June 2027. Without this intervention, the price cap would have been set around £45 higher.

To better target support, we are working across Government to join up public sector data. The Energy Independence Bill will also broaden the existing gateway for data sharing between Government and energy licence holders beyond fuel poverty, where appropriate. This could help target future support at people facing high energy costs, living in hard-to-heat homes or with higher energy needs, while maintaining existing data protection safeguards.

Our Fuel Poverty Strategy for England and Warm Homes Plan will reduce energy costs for low-income households and aim to lift up to one million households out of fuel poverty by 2030.

Lower and middle-income pensioners will also benefit from Winter Fuel Payments, with payments recovered through the tax system from those with annual incomes above £35,000.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what safeguards exist to prevent clinical staff from downgrading parental concerns on electronic Patient Wellness Assessments.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care

answeringMember.name: Dame Diana Johnson
answeringMember.memberFrom: Kingston upon Hull North and Cottingham

writtenQuestions.answerText:
Parents who feel their concerns about their child’s condition have been downgraded on the electronic Patient Wellness Assessments or are not being acted on can use Martha’s Rule to request a review by a different team at any time. This route is also available to patients, their families, and carers.

This route is one of three components that safeguard against concerns being overlooked under Martha’s Rule. The other safeguards are:

  • patient wellness questions, for which patients are asked at least daily about how they are feeling and whether they are getting better or worse, so that staff can act on their answers in a structured way; and

  • staff can also request a review by a different team at any time if they are concerned that a patient is deteriorating and their concerns are not being acted on.

The patient wellness questions are also built into the national paediatric early warning system to support a structured response to concerns raised by patients or parents. Data on the use of Martha’s Rule is available at the following link:

https://www.england.nhs.uk/statistics/statistical-work-areas/marthas-rule/

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what guidance governs the consideration of immigration detention for foreign nationals with previous overseas terrorism convictions where removal cannot immediately be effected; and what arrangements are in place to assess the use of (a) immigration detention, (b) electronic monitoring, (c) curfews and reporting requirements and (d) Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures where the respective statutory criteria are met.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Decisions on immigration detention are made on a case-by-case basis in accordance with the Detention General Instructions, and account for all relevant circumstances, including, but not limited to, the prospects of removal and risk of harm to the public.

Where immigration bail is granted, the Immigration Bail guidance provides for appropriate conditions to be imposed. These may include reporting, electronic monitoring, and curfews. Conditions are determined on a case-by-case basis, taking account of the risks presented, including national security concerns.

The Extremism and Radicalisation Detention Services Order sets out arrangements for identifying and referring concerns about extremism and radicalisation across the immigration removal estate. Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures (TPIMs) can be imposed to manage the terrorism-related risk posed by an individual, including a foreign national. Each case is considered on its individual circumstances, and a TPIM may only be imposed where the statutory conditions in the TPIM Act 2011 are met.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what steps they are taking to require safeguarding features in discrete wearable filming technologies.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises the risks presented by technologies that enable images, video and information to be captured discreetly and hands-free, including wearable filming technologies.

We are clear that the benefits of these technologies must be weighed against the harm that can be caused, including where they are misused to facilitate harmful behaviour.

The Government expects technology companies to design and deploy products responsibly, with privacy and safety considerations built in from the outset. We will consider whether existing safeguards and regulatory frameworks adequately address product features that may facilitate harmful or deceptive uses.

Where technologies create risks of harm or misuse, effective safeguards are needed, and we will consider the full range of appropriate and possible measures. All options remain on the table as we consider how best to manage these risks.

More broadly, through the Government's Freedom from Violence and Abuse: A Cross-Government Strategy, we have committed to consider what more we can do to encourage the ‘safety by design’ of smart and connected technology to better protect victims and survivors and help stop perpetrators using this type of technology to further their abuse.

writtenStatements.title: Water customer support and advocacy
writtenStatements.text:
I am updating the House on the steps this Government is taking to give water customers a stronger voice and help low-income households with high essential water needs with their bills. Customers in receipt of benefits such as Pension Credit and who cannot cut their water use due to their circumstances, such as medical conditions, are eligible for support but many simply aren’t getting it.

For too long, water companies have let people down. Bills are rising, performance is falling short and trust in water companies has reached a record low.

Customers deserve a reliable service, fair treatment, value for money and greater support for those who need it. Our programme of reform will put these priorities at the heart of a fairer, more efficient and more affordable water system, delivering lasting improvements in service while minimising the impact on bills.

This Government is taking forward three practical steps. A stronger, independent Water Watchdog will stand up for customers. Simpler access to WaterSure will help eligible households with their bills. A Water Charter will help customers understand their rights and what they should expect from their water company.

A stronger voice for water customers

As the Prime Minister has made clear, essential services must be accountable to the people who rely on them. Rebuilding trust in the water sector means giving consumers a stronger voice and holding water companies to account for the services they provide.

Recognising the importance of a dedicated consumer advocate, we will strengthen the Consumer Council for Water (CCW) into a new Water Watchdog. This will give people in England and Wales a stronger, independent voice focused solely on their interests, with new powers to investigate and address poor service and emerging issues before they become widespread.

The Water Watchdog will champion the public across the water system, advising people on areas including their customer rights, affordability support and water efficiency. It will undertake research, run consumer panels and assess companies' customer service. Where a customer complaint cannot be resolved by their water company, the new Water Ombudsman will provide independent, impartial and legally binding decisions. Together, these bodies will improve water companies’ customer service, tackle the root causes of complaints and give people confidence that their concerns will be heard and resolved. These outcomes will be the basis on which we judge the success of the new framework and its contribution to restoring trust.

Helping households with their water bills

We are also making it easier for vulnerable households in England and Wales to get help with their water bills.

WaterSure caps bills for eligible households that need to use more water because of a medical condition or the needs of a larger family. This support can make a real difference to households under financial pressure.

Government research shows that as many as 250,000 more households are eligible for WaterSure but are missing out because they do not know support is available. We want to make sure they get the help they are entitled to.

We will work with water companies and the Department for Work and Pensions to use data sharing to identify households in England and Wales who may qualify for WaterSure. Companies will then contact these eligible households directly to explain the support available and help them apply, streamlining the application process to make it as easy as possible. For those already eligible, if there have been no changes in circumstances, they will just be re-enrolled rather than having to reapply. Together, these steps will help people access support they are already entitled to and give customers breathing space with the cost of living.

Water Charter

The steps this Government has taken have given people a stronger voice and stronger protections. However, information on people’s rights, protections and available support is spread across different sources and can be hard to find, leaving too many people unclear about what they are entitled to.

The new Water Charter will address this by bringing that information together in one clear and accessible place. It will set out what customers should expect from their water company, and the support and redress available when things go wrong.

With complaints rising and trust in the sector low, the Charter will help people challenge companies when their rights are not met and hold them to account to get the support they are entitled to.

Conclusion

Trust in the water sector will be rebuilt through action, not promises.

This Government is delivering a Water Watchdog that stands up for customers and challenges companies’ failures, easier access to WaterSure for households who need help with their bills, and a Water Charter that helps customers understand and use their rights. Together, these steps will help put customers first.
